senses.gloss: That which is called {{word}}; the thing or quality so named. (invented for layout)
The state or condition of being {{word}}; hence, figuratively, any state resembling it.
A person or thing remarkable for {{word}}; one given to it.
To make or become {{word}}; to render such.

entry.body:
{{WORD}}, a subject on which the eleventh edition would spend four hundred words of confident Edwardian prose before conceding, in its last sentence, that the matter is disputed.

> The article's own citation would sit here, set smaller, and would name a German monograph nobody has opened since 1904.

*(invented for layout)*

when something is so {{word}} that saying it once doesn't cover it. deployed in the group chat, never out loud.

> “not the {{word}} behaviour again”

*(invented for layout)*

evidence.label: TIKTOK
evidence.body: POV: you look up {{word}} and the dictionary is meaner than you are

evidence.label: TWEET
evidence.body: every generation invents a word for {{word}} and every generation thinks it invented the thing

evidence.label: SONG LYRIC
evidence.body: “and the {{word}} of it lived rent-free / somewhere behind my teeth”

evidence.label: YOUTUBE
evidence.body: How to spot {{word}} in the wild — a video essay

evidence.label: INSTAGRAM · CAROUSEL
evidence.body: six slides on {{word}}, five of them a beige apartment

evidence.label: COMMUNITY EXAMPLE
evidence.body: Nominated as an example of {{word}}: a person, with a Wikidata item of their own, so the example is a link between two things rather than a caption.

senses.gloss: Any marine bivalve mollusk of the genus Ostrea. They are usually found adhering to rocks or other fixed objects. (invented for layout)
A small mass of dark meat found in a cavity of the bone on each side of the back of a fowl.
A person of few words; one from whom nothing may be got.

entry.body:
OYSTER, the common name of the lamellibranch molluscs of the family *Ostreidae*, of which the eleventh edition treats at length, with a plate, and with a digression on the beds of Whitstable that runs to a column and a half.

> The oyster is, of all shell-fish, that which has been longest cultivated by man; the Romans, as Pliny relates, esteemed those of Brundisium above all others.

*(invented for layout)*

the sea's way of testing your commitment. you don't like them, you like *having eaten* them.

> “he ordered a dozen oysters to seem like a man with a boat”

*(invented for layout)*

evidence.label: TIKTOK
evidence.body: shucking my first oyster and immediately regretting the whole 19th century

evidence.label: TWEET
evidence.body: the world is your oyster is a threat if you have ever actually met an oyster

evidence.label: SONG LYRIC
evidence.body: “I will not lend thee a penny — / why then the world's mine oyster, / which I with sword will open”

evidence.label: YOUTUBE
evidence.body: The oyster beds that fed London, and the winter that killed them

evidence.label: INSTAGRAM
evidence.body: half a dozen on ice, one lemon, no context

evidence.label: COMMUNITY EXAMPLE
evidence.body: Nominated as an example of “oyster”: the Whitstable Oyster Festival, a thing with a Wikidata item, linked to the thing the word names rather than to the string.

senses.gloss: Any animal belonging to the natural family Felidae, and in particular to the various species of the genera Felis, Panthera, and Lynx. (invented for layout)
A strong vessel with a narrow stern, projecting quarters, and a deep waist, used in the coal and timber trade.
A double tripod having six legs, so contrived that whichever way it falls it stands upon three.

entry.body:
CAT (*Felis domestica*), on which the eleventh edition is unusually warm, allowing the animal three columns and conceding, against its own habit, that the creature is agreeable company.

> Of the domestication of the cat in Egypt there can be no doubt; the mummied remains found at Beni-Hasan are numbered in tens of thousands.

*(invented for layout)*

a small landlord you are legally required to feed.

> “my cat has never once acknowledged the rent”

*(invented for layout)*

evidence.body: he sits like a man who has read the lease

evidence.label: TWEET

evidence.label: SONG LYRIC

senses.gloss: The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness; exhilaration of spirits. (invented for layout)
That which causes joy or happiness; the cause or occasion of gladness.
To rejoice; to be glad; to delight; to exult.

entry.body:
JOY, treated by the eleventh edition not under its own head but within the article on the *Emotions*, where it is defined against grief and then largely abandoned in favour of a discussion of the vasomotor system.

> The physiologists are agreed that the expression of joy is the more difficult to counterfeit, the eye being less obedient than the mouth.

*(invented for layout)*

the feeling you get about a thing before you find out what it costs.

> “pure joy, briefly, and then the invoice”

*(invented for layout)*
